title: Final Project: ARS and GA
markdown:
## What this covers

STAT243 ("Introduction to Statistical Computing," UC Berkeley) closes with a group project rather
than a final exam: a piece of software, built and tested the way the rest of the course argued
software should be built and tested. This chapter is not a lecture — it is the project brief
itself, in the three versions it survives in: Fall 2024's adaptive-rejection-sampling package, and
the genetic-algorithm-for-variable-selection package set in both Fall 2021 (in R) and Fall 2025 (in
Python). Read together, the three briefs are a single, worked statement of what the course meant by
"good scientific software" — modularity, testing under randomness, vectorizing what can be
vectorized, and documenting for a user who is not the author — applied twice, to two different
algorithms. It assumes familiarity with the course's running themes on package structure, testing,
and vectorization/parallelization; it does not explain adaptive rejection sampling or genetic
algorithms themselves, since the briefs point elsewhere for that (see Sources).

## The shape every year shares

Every version of the project has the same skeleton. Groups of three are assigned at random. The
project is "not intended to be a huge undertaking" once split three ways, but it is graded as a
letter grade worth about two problem sets (or problem sets/quizzes), so it counts for real. Students
may cite and consult papers, code, online resources — and, from Fall 2024 on, chatbots — but not
classmates outside their group; the instructors (Chris or João) are always fair game. The deliverable
always has two parts: a package with a specified primary function, supporting modules, `pytest` (or
`testthat`) tests the grader can run unmodified, and a docstring/help page for the primary function
with a worked, runnable example — plus a short write-up (a 2–4 page PDF in 2024, a README in 2025)
that describes the design, the testing, and, always, **a paragraph naming which team member did
which part**. Both years recommend the same workflow: map out the modular pieces and the interface
before writing code, have a second person test and improve whatever the first person wrote (or pair
program), and use Git/GitHub throughout rather than at the end.

Two requirements recur verbatim because they are the hard part of every one of these algorithms:

- **The core algorithm is inherently sequential** — rejection sampling refines its envelope one
  accepted or rejected point at a time; a genetic algorithm's generations feed into each other — so
  "vectorize as much as possible" and "parallelize what genuinely doesn't depend on the sequence"
  (multiple sample points at once for ARS; the cross-validation folds, or the population's fitness
  evaluations within one generation, for the GA) is the recurring efficiency instruction, not "make
  it fast" in general.
- **The algorithm is stochastic, so testing it is not a matter of checking an exact answer.** All
  three briefs flag this as something requiring real thought: compare samples, or selected variable
  sets, to a known distribution or a known truth using appropriate statistical checks, and back that
  up with ordinary unit tests of the deterministic sub-computations that make up the algorithm.

## Case study: adaptive rejection sampling (Fall 2024)

The task: a Python package, `ars`, whose primary function `ars(...)` implements the adaptive
rejection sampler "described in the Unit 9 notes (Section 5) and with details in Section 2.2 of
Gilks et al. (1992)" — neither of which is part of this brief; see Sources. The grading criteria are
specific about what the *interface* to that algorithm has to guarantee, even though the algorithm's
internals are left to the cited sources:

1. The primary input is a (possibly unnormalized) density function, supplied vectorized "in a
   fashion" like a `scipy` pdf, plus the number of samples wanted; inputs are validated. Rather than
   a general a-priori test that the density is log-concave, the code has to catch log-concavity
   failures numerically *as the sampler runs* — specifically, it has to notice if the upper and
   lower bounding functions the algorithm builds are not actually bounding the density.
2. Testing compares samples to the true distribution, which — since the output is stochastic —
   "will require some thought," and part of the grade rests on how the package performs against
   densities the instructor supplies, not just the ones the group chose to try. Individual
   non-trivial computations get their own unit tests.
3. Modular code, one consistent style (functions or OOP, pick one) throughout.
4. Vectorize as much as the sequential structure allows; consider generating several sample points
   per pass.
5. Complete documentation.
6. Gradients start from numerical differentiation. A top ("A") solution adds automatic
   differentiation via JAX or PyTorch — used here purely for its differentiation, not for GPU
   throughput, since "we can't set up this problem to do a large number of identical calculations at
   once."
7. `scipy`/`numpy`/`jax`/`pytorch` are fair game as building blocks; using or imitating an existing
   ARS implementation found online is not.

The package is developed in a private repository (`ars-dev`) shared with the instructor, and the
write-up — a 2–4 page Quarto-rendered PDF, submitted on paper with the repository URL written on it
— covers the design, the testing, and the results on example densities.

## Case study: genetic algorithms for variable selection (Fall 2021 and Fall 2025)

Both years point to the same source for the algorithm itself — Section 3.4 of Givens and Hoeting,
*Computational Statistics* — and to the book's own baseball example as a worked case (Fall 2025
supplies the actual dataset, `project/baseball.dat`). What changes between the two offerings is the
interface the package has to expose and the fitness criterion it optimizes, and the differences are
informative about where the course's expectations moved.

**Fall 2021, in R.** The package `GA` exposes a function `select(...)` that takes a dataset and a
regression type, passing most of that straight to `lm()`/`glm()`. The default objective is AIC, but
the user can supply a custom objective, and — while the default genetic operators follow Givens and
Hoeting — the code should ideally let a user supply additional ones. Results are demonstrated on at
least two examples, shown directly in the R help page's example section. Aside from model fitting
and other functionality in base R and its bundled `stats` package, the group writes its own code;
anything else needs the instructor's sign-off first. The deliverable is an installable package
(`R CMD build`/`INSTALL`, or `install_github`), tests runnable via `testthat::test_package('GA')`
and checked to work outside the development environment, and a `select.Rd` help page (hand-written
or generated with `roxygen2`).

**Fall 2025, in Python.** The package `GA` exposes `select(...)`, but now must additionally *conform
to the input/output interface of an instructor-supplied template repository*
(`github.com/paciorek/GA-dev`) — extra arguments and extra output-dictionary entries are allowed,
but the required ones must be there, precisely so the instructor is not adapting to a different
interface for every group. The fitness function is now fixed and explicit: 10-fold
cross-validated $R^2$,

$$R^2 = 1 - \frac{\text{summed squared prediction error}}{\text{sum of squared deviations around the
mean of the observations}}.$$

Because some prediction methods have built-in regularization and may not actually zero out unused
predictors, a `penalty` argument $\lambda$ is required, with the penalized fitness

$$R^2 - \lambda f, \qquad f = \text{fraction of potential predictors selected},$$

and the instructor will apply this with a "moderate" $\lambda$ on some grading cases — the default
GA, with the default prediction method, is expected to find a reasonably sparse good set of
predictors under it. Parallelism is explicitly scoped: cross-validation is the one piece that
parallelizes trivially within a sequential run of generations, and any parallel processing (of the
CV, or of fitness evaluation across the population) must be gated by a required `n_workers` argument
defaulting to `1`. The group must get a plain linear-regression version working first before moving
to a more interesting prediction method — which "provides the opportunity for one or more group
members to explore other methods that might be of interest to them." The code must pass the tests
in the `GA-dev` template (via GitHub Actions or by hand; `assess.py` gives a quick local check), and
the brief is explicit that this is "not a bake-off": grading rewards *reasonable* performance and
run-time under the default settings, not the best achievable $R^2$. AI assistance is allowed but
scoped tightly — "limit it to brainstorming and help with small components," with the structural
decisions (functional vs. OOP, function/method choices, arguments) made by the humans and any
AI-touched code checked and understood before submission. The write-up moves from a separate PDF to
a README (optionally authored as `README.qmd` and rendered), and submission is via a Google form
rather than a paper copy.

## What the two case studies share

Different algorithm, different language, same underlying discipline: one function is the public
contract (`ars`, `select`); everything else is a private, modular, individually-tested
implementation behind it; the stochastic output is validated statistically rather than checked
against an exact number; the one place where real speed is available (multiple points at once for
ARS, the CV folds or population evaluation for GA) is vectorized or explicitly, optionally
parallelized rather than parallelized by default; documentation is written for a user who did not
write the code; and the boundary of "code you may use" is drawn tightly — named numerical libraries
in, anything that reimplements the algorithm itself out — with an explicit, and over time more
detailed, obligation to say where any outside idea, including an AI's, came from.

## Exercises

The following are the course's own project tasks, restated; neither is solved here.

1. **Adaptive rejection sampling.** Implement a Python package `ars` whose primary function samples
   from a user-supplied (possibly unnormalized) log-concave density, following the design in the
   Fall 2024 brief above: validated inputs, numerical checks that catch a non-log-concave density
   during sampling, formal tests against known distributions (plus unit tests of the
   sub-computations), vectorization/batched sampling where the sequential structure allows it,
   gradients by numerical differentiation with automatic differentiation (JAX or PyTorch) as an
   extension, and documentation with a runnable example. Do not use or adapt an existing ARS
   implementation.

2. **Genetic algorithm for variable selection.** Implement a package that selects predictors for a
   regression model by a genetic algorithm, in either of the two forms above: an R package `GA`
   with a `select()` function defaulting to AIC as its objective (Fall 2021 form), or a Python
   package `GA` with a `select()` function conforming to a fixed interface, using 10-fold
   cross-validated $R^2$ — optionally penalized by $R^2 - \lambda f$ against the fraction of
   predictors selected — as its fitness criterion, with parallelism gated behind an `n_workers`
   argument (Fall 2025 form). Get a plain linear-regression version working before trying a more
   elaborate prediction method. Demonstrate the result on at least two examples, and test the
   overall (stochastic) procedure against a known truth as well as unit-testing its pieces.
